global.headline: IRAN'S DRAFT HORMUZ PLAN WOULD BAR US AND ISRAELI SHIPS AS WASHINGTON REJECTS ANY TOLLS; ISRAEL LOSES FIRST LEBANON TROOPS SINCE JUNE TRUCE; HOUTHIS KILL 30+ IN YEMEN'S WORST ESCALATION SINCE 2022
summary: Iran's proposed terms for a new Strait of Hormuz shipping arrangement with Oman — nearing what Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi called its "final stage" after three-plus weeks of talks — would route inbound vessels through Iranian territorial waters and outbound traffic via a corridor closer to Oman, replacing the pre-war route through Omani waters entirely and closing the temporary passage near Iran's Larak Island used since the ceasefire. But a draft circulated by Iranian state outlet Fars would explicitly bar US and Israeli-flagged or -linked vessels from transiting at all, while Tehran is separately pushing a 5-7% cargo-value transit fee (Oman has proposed 3%) that Gharibabadi said depends on "the country's highest authorities" and on US conduct. Washington rejected the terms almost immediately: a US official told CNBC any temporary route "will be without any impediments — meaning no approvals or permissions and no tolls or charges," calling Hormuz "an international waterway [which] no party controls." Trump and Treasury Secretary Bessent had said a deal could land by Wednesday or Thursday; Brent crude held little-changed near $83.64 a barrel Thursday morning, a market still waiting for actual signed terms rather than another round of dueling claims.

In Lebanon, Israeli reservists Harel Birenstock and Tamir Vaknin were killed and four more soldiers seriously wounded Thursday when they entered a booby-trapped building in the southern village of Majdal Zoun — the first Israeli military deaths since the June truce with Hezbollah took hold. Israel's military said it responded with "precise strikes" across the south over what it called a "blatant violation of the ceasefire," including a strike that hit the roof of a cemetery prayer hall in Tibnin, killing one person and injuring 12; a separate strike on Burj Shemali wounded eight more. The seventh round of US-brokered Israel-Lebanon talks in Rome continued regardless; State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott called the technical-level talks "fruitful" and said both sides were "much closer" to agreeing on expanding pilot withdrawal zones, though Lebanon said it still had no answer from Israel on renewing and fully implementing the ceasefire itself.

Separately, Iran-aligned Houthi rebels launched missile and drone strikes Thursday on camps of Yemen's internationally recognised, Saudi-backed government forces in the central Marib and Hadramawt provinces, killing at least 30 troops per Yemeni officials (other reports put it as high as 45) and wounding dozens more — described by analysts as the fiercest Yemen military escalation since 2022. Casualties were unusually high because troops had gathered for a morning training exercise when the attack hit, according to Yemen's First Emergency Division Command; Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree claimed the strikes caused "hundreds" of casualties.
global.geopolitical: Iran's draft plan to bar the two parties most central to the war it wants to end — the US and Israel — from a strait it is simultaneously trying to reopen shows the fee-and-permission framework taking shape is not the neutral reopening markets have assumed, but another vehicle for the same free-transit-versus-supervisory-control standoff that has scuttled every prior mediation; Lebanon's first Israeli combat deaths since June, arriving the same day Rome's technical track was pronounced "fruitful," confirm diplomatic progress on paper and renewed violence on the ground continue to run on entirely separate, uncoordinated timelines; and Yemen's worst Houthi-government clash since 2022, opening a third active front tied to the same Iran-aligned network, shows how far the regional war's reach now extends beyond the strait and Lebanon combined.
global.socioeconomic: An unsigned deal that would exclude the war's principal antagonists from Hormuz gives oil markets little reason to price in a genuine reopening even if Iran and Oman finalise terms, since two of the vessel classes at the heart of the underlying dispute would remain barred regardless; Lebanon's south faces a fresh cycle of displacement and property damage just as families had hoped Rome's momentum might finally deliver an end to the recurring strikes; and Yemen's newly bereaved military communities absorb another blow to an economy already hollowed out by a decade of civil war and blockade.

global.headline: UKRAINE HITS TWO MAJOR RUSSIAN REFINERIES DEEP INSIDE RUSSIA AS NATO RACES TO GET KYIV AIR DEFENCES; LEIPZIG DRONE BOMB FOUND NEAR UKRAINIAN AMMUNITION FLIGHT
summary: Ukraine's forces struck two major oil refineries deep inside Russian territory overnight — the Bashneft-Novoil plant roughly 950 miles away in Bashkortostan and the Slavneft-YANOS refinery in Yaroslavl, 270 miles northeast of Moscow and one of Russia's five largest, with an annual crude capacity of 15 million tonnes — using more than 600 drones in what Ukraine's General Staff called one of its largest single-night strike packages. Footage showed a large fire at the Yaroslavl site. President Volodymyr Zelensky said the strikes "once again worked to limit Russia's oil revenues, which it uses to finance the war and the killing of Ukrainians," extending a campaign Kyiv says has already cut Russia's refining capacity by roughly 20%.

The strikes followed NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte saying, after speaking with Zelensky, that he is "discussing with Allies how we can continue to get Ukraine the air defences they urgently need" — after Kyiv failed to shoot down a single one of the ballistic missiles Russia fired in Wednesday's deadly barrage, a first this year. Zelensky, addressing a National Security and Defense Council meeting on winter resilience, warned Moscow is significantly ramping up missile production ahead of winter, and did not rule out that stalled Western interceptor supplies were "aimed at making Ukraine ... more willing to compromise" in any peace talks.

Separately, German investigators confirmed the explosive-laden drone found near Leipzig/Halle airport Wednesday was discovered metres from a Ukrainian aircraft loaded with military ammunition, according to a classified police report cited by public broadcasters WDR, NDR and the Süddeutsche Zeitung; a minister said a "ripped" detonator narrowly averted "a catastrophe with multiple casualties." Germany is now investigating whether a foreign state was involved.
global.geopolitical: Ukraine's deep-strike campaign against Russia's largest refineries — now including one of its top five plants — shows Kyiv's offensive reach into Russian rear-area infrastructure is outpacing Moscow's ability to defend it, even as Ukraine's own cities remain critically exposed to exactly the kind of missile barrage that killed 17 people Wednesday; Rutte's "urgently" framing signals NATO itself now treats the interceptor gap as an alliance-level failure rather than simply a Ukrainian supply problem, while the confirmed Ukrainian-ammunition target at Leipzig sharpens the sabotage campaign's reach onto NATO soil into something more than an isolated drone discovery.
global.socioeconomic: Slavneft-YANOS's 15-million-tonne annual capacity makes it one of the more consequential refineries yet knocked offline, compounding the fuel-supply strain already visible domestically inside Russia; Ukraine's own exposure runs the other way — NATO's "urgent" scramble for interceptors underscores how thin its air-defence stockpile has worn after repeated large-scale barrages — while a foreign-state-backed plot against a Ukrainian ammunition flight, if confirmed, would impose a fresh, uninsurable risk on NATO's own civil-aviation infrastructure.

global.headline: NIGERIA RESCUES 308 ABDUCTEES IN COUNTRY'S LARGEST-EVER SINGLE-DAY HOSTAGE OPERATION
summary: Nigerian security forces — a joint operation involving the military, police, the Department of State Services and the National Counter-Terrorism Centre — rescued 308 people abducted in separate attacks across Niger and Kwara states, recovering them from militant hideouts deep in the forests of Kainji Lake National Park. Of those freed, 163 were taken in February's mass abduction from Woro village in Kwara state, where gunmen killed more than 150 people and seized an unknown number of captives near the border with Benin; the remaining 145 were abducted separately in Niger State. President Bola Ahmed Tinubu hailed the operation as the largest single-day hostage rescue in the country's history, according to presidential spokesman Bayo Onanuga.
global.geopolitical: A rescue of this scale is a rare, unambiguous security-forces success against Nigeria's chronic mass-kidnapping economy, but the nearly six-month gap between the Woro abduction and Thursday's recovery also shows how long armed groups can hold captives undetected in forest terrain the state still struggles to police, even with a dedicated counter-terrorism command involved.
global.socioeconomic: Recovering 308 captives in one operation removes a significant share of the ransom-driven kidnapping economy's current captive pool, but does nothing to address the underlying insecurity across north-central Nigeria's forest belt that has made mass abduction a routine, comparatively low-risk revenue stream for militant groups operating there.

global.headline: DRC EBOLA OUTBREAK NEARS 4,000 CASES AS CONGO RIVER BOAT IS QUARANTINED, VIRUS MUTATION FEARED
summary: The Democratic Republic of Congo placed a Congo River passenger boat under quarantine Thursday after five onboard deaths linked to Ebola, with all passengers now being screened as a precaution, the health minister said — as the country's Bundibugyo-strain outbreak approached 4,000 confirmed cases (3,874 cases and 1,751 deaths as of 4 August, per the latest available tally). Africa's public health watchdog, the Africa CDC, said the time for "incremental action" was over and announced plans to scale up every part of the response, including door-to-door case-finding, after health officials raised concern the virus itself may be mutating.
global.geopolitical: A boat placed under quarantine after onboard deaths shows the outbreak has outrun the contact-tracing capacity that controlled past Ebola flare-ups, forcing authorities onto a reactive, incident-by-incident footing even as WHO and Africa CDC try to shift to proactive door-to-door searches; a confirmed mutation would sharpen the already-acute problem that existing vaccines and treatments are certified only against the Zaire strain, not the Bundibugyo strain driving this outbreak.
global.socioeconomic: With cases nearing 4,000 and deaths above 1,750 barely three months in, the outbreak is inflicting a rising toll on a health system already strained by years of underinvestment and conflict in eastern DRC, and river-transport quarantines risk choking off one of the region's few reliable trade and supply corridors.

global.headline: CEUTA DEATH TOLL CONFIRMED AT 100+ AS EU FLAGS ONLINE CALLS FOR A REPEAT BORDER SURGE ON AUG 15
summary: Ceuta's mayor-president Juan Jesús Vivas told the European Parliament's civil liberties committee in Brussels on Thursday that at least 100 people died during the late-July mass border crossing from Morocco — up sharply from the 72 reported just three days earlier — with 3,000 to 5,000 migrants still in the Spanish enclave after roughly 80,000 crossed on 30-31 July. Vivas said Ceuta's two reception centres had "collapsed" under the strain. A European Commission spokesperson said the bloc was aware of social-media posts calling for a repeat crossing attempt on 15 August and had set up an operational group preparing for possible impacts.
global.geopolitical: A confirmed toll of at least 100 — up from 72 just days earlier — turns Ceuta from an acute one-off surge into one of the deadliest single migration events at an EU external border in years, and open online calls for a repeat on 15 August will test whether Spain and the EU's post-crisis reinforcement measures have actually closed the underlying vulnerability or merely reacted to the first wave.
global.socioeconomic: With thousands still stranded in an enclave whose reception system has "collapsed," Ceuta faces a protracted humanitarian and fiscal strain well beyond the initial crossing itself, and a credible threat of a second surge on 15 August would test Spain's capacity to prevent a repeat rather than simply having absorbed one shock.

singapore.headline: MAN DEPORTED FROM MALAYSIA TO BE CHARGED FOR INSULTING ISLAM IN VIRAL VIDEOS
summary: A 27-year-old man will be charged in a Singapore court on Friday under the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act for uploading social media videos containing insulting and profane remarks about the Muslim community, police said. He had already left Singapore by the time a member of the public lodged a police report on 1 March; with the assistance of the Royal Malaysia Police, he was deported from Malaysia and arrested on arrival in Singapore on Thursday. He faces up to five years' jail, a fine, or both if convicted. Separately, he is assisting police with an unrelated investigation into a different viral video showing a man stepping on a copy of the Quran.
singapore.geopolitical: The case is a purely domestic prosecution, but its resolution — via deportation coordinated with Malaysian police rather than a Singapore-led extradition process — is a small, functional example of the routine bilateral law-enforcement cooperation that lets Singapore still reach suspects who leave the country ahead of a police report.
singapore.socioeconomic: The charge keeps religious-harmony enforcement firmly in the news, reinforcing that online remarks deemed insulting to a religious community continue to draw swift, serious prosecution regardless of where the poster is by the time a report is made.

singapore.headline: SINGAPORE FINDS NO EVIDENCE OF LOCAL OFFENCE IN INDONESIAN BABY-TRAFFICKING RING, BUT CAN'T IDENTIFY NAMED AGENTS
summary: Singapore authorities have found no evidence that an offence was committed here, or by Singapore-based adoption agents, in connection with an Indonesian baby-trafficking ring that sent infants to Singapore for adoption, the Straits Times reported Thursday — even as West Java authorities allege three Singapore-based adoption agents were involved. Prosecutors said they have not been able to identify the specific agents operating in Singapore, leaving no clear way to trace what became of the babies placed through them. A Bandung court sentenced 19 ring members on 21 July to jail terms of between three years four months and seven years for trafficking at least 34 babies between 2023 and 2025, each allegedly sold for S$14,300 to roughly S$17,900 (200 million to 250 million rupiah).
singapore.geopolitical: The gap between Indonesia's specific allegation — naming three Singapore-based agents — and Singapore's finding of no local offence, compounded by prosecutors' own admission they cannot identify those agents, leaves an accountability vacuum neither country's investigation currently closes, complicating what should otherwise be a straightforward cross-border case given Indonesia's own convictions are already secured.
singapore.socioeconomic: Adoptive families in Singapore who took in children through the ring now face a case that may never establish exactly how their children were obtained, while the unresolved question of whether any Singapore-based intermediary profited from a trafficking operation leaves the local adoption-facilitation sector's own oversight gaps unaddressed.

singapore.headline: MOM UNVEILS ENHANCED MIGRANT-WORKER HEALTHCARE PLAN: CLINICS WITHIN 2KM, FOUR ANCHOR OPERATORS FROM APRIL 2027
summary: The Ministry of Manpower will roll out an enhanced Primary Care Plan for migrant workers from 1 April 2027, appointing four Anchor Operators to run a consolidated network of 22 clinics organised into four geographic zones — bringing most workers within 2km of a clinic, down from 3km under the current scheme. Co-payments for both physical consultations and telemedicine will be standardised at S$5, and MOM will launch a centralised portal for employers to enrol workers and manage their coverage, alongside enhanced booking systems letting workers make, change or cancel appointments themselves.
singapore.geopolitical: As a purely domestic administrative reform, the plan carries no cross-border dimension, though it is one more incremental improvement layered onto Singapore's decade-long build-out of dedicated migrant-worker healthcare infrastructure since the original Primary Care Plan launched in 2022.
singapore.socioeconomic: Halving the effective travel distance to care and standardising co-payments should meaningfully improve access for a workforce with historically uneven healthcare utilisation, while shifting enrolment and scheduling onto a centralised digital portal should reduce the administrative burden employers currently bear managing coverage across dispersed clinic networks.

word.definition: An act of retaliation against another party, especially a military response to a perceived wrong or violation, often disproportionate to the original act.
word.etymology: From Old French reprisaille and medieval Latin reprensalia (from reprendere, "to take back, seize again"), originally denoting the seizure of goods or persons in retaliation for a wrong done to one's countrymen; entered English in the 15th century via French maritime and legal usage, later broadening to any retaliatory act.
word.example: Israel's military framed Thursday's strikes across southern Lebanon explicitly as reprisal for the ceasefire violation it blamed for killing reservists Harel Birenstock and Tamir Vaknin — even as, by the US State Department's own account, the Rome talks meant to end precisely this kind of retaliatory cycle were turning "fruitful" the very same day.
